newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Strong profit growth seen for UK firms.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Strong profit growth seen for UK firms.

text.p: UK company earnings are set to surge in 1997, fuelled by Britain's strong economy, while dividends stay at attractive levels, equities strategists say.

Strategists at a handful of top international investment banks say increased consumer spending in Britain could push corporate earnings into double digit growth from its estimated single-digit level this year.

"As we look at next year, we're looking at an accelerating economy. Sterling's probably peaked, and we'd be quite bullish that earnings are going to grow healthily," said Andrew Bell, head of investment trust research at BZW.
BZW sees earnings rising by 11 percent in 1997 after an estimated increase of 6.0 percent this year, while other investment banks are even more optimistic.
Richard Davidson, European equities strategist at Morgan Stanley, said he expects earnings growth to reach 15 percent next year after 11 percent in 1996.
"We feel quite comfortable with that number. I think there's a big underestimation of UK earnings," he said, predicting that strong GDP growth and consumer spending would fuel the rise.
The forecast increase in earnings means that profits growth at UK companies will probably outpace that of their U.S. counterparts but lag most of Europe.
"The main explanation is the different points of the economic cycle," said Peter Sullivan, European equities strategist at Goldman Sachs.
"Europe's still in the relatively early stages of a pickup, and you tend to get stronger profits," he added.
STURDY DIVIDEND GROWTH SEEN
Most strategists predict sturdy dividends in 1997, although their forecasts differ after heady payouts from utilities and oil firms boosted overall dividend growth this year.
Steve Wright, equities strategist at BZW, expects dividend growth to decline to seven percent next year from his estimate of nine percent for 1996.

"You've had a balance of companies that are delivering very little dividend growth, and some that are delivering 25 percent. So it's more the effect of those very big ones dropping out than of everyone paying less," he said.
However, Goldman's Sullivan sees dividend growth rising to 10 percent in 1997 from about six percent this year, citing the advanced stage of the UK's economic recovery.
"You tend to get a pickup in dividend growth after earnings growth has gone past its peak, and we expect to see that pattern again this time," he said.
FTSE 100 SEEN POSTING MODEST GAINS
The earnings and dividend outlook should help the bellwether FTSE 100 index post modest gains in 1997, barring any massive corrections in global stock markets, most strategists say.

Davidson recommended overweighting UK equities relative to the rest of Europe and the U.S., but added that he expects the FTSE 100 to reach only 4,100 points by year-end 1997, little changed from its present level of around 4,000.
"That's about the most upside I'm predicting for any European stock market next year," he said, predicting that the region's markets would fall 10 percent on average next year.
But some strategists say UK stocks look fully-valued, arguing that profits will tail off after 1997, making the market's current price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 14 times hard to justify.
Goldman's Sullivan said he recently trimmed his earnings growth forecast for 1997 to 13 percent from 15 percent -- versus 6.0 percent this year -- to reflect sterling's strength.

"Even with the relatively strong earnings growth, the valuations suggest there's little upside. So we're underweight (UK stocks) in European and global portfolios," he said, noting that his 12-month forecast for the FTSE 100 was 3,950.
LITTLE RISK SEEN FROM STERLING STRENGTH, UK ELECTION
Like Sullivan, most strategists expect economic strength to offset the negative effect of sterling's rise, while recovery in the rest of Europe should give a boost to British exporters.

"The strength of the pound is certainly a risk, but I think a lot of that is taken into account. In fact, I think it might be beneficial in controlling interest rate moves," said Davidson at Morgan Stanley.
The prospect of a win by the opposition Labour Party at the next general election poses little threat to corporate earnings outside the utilities sector, strategists say.

The Labour Party has wooed the investment community with reassurances that its economic and fiscal policy will be responsible. However, it is now 17 years since Labour was last in power and future policy specifics are still sparse.
Poll-leading Labour has vowed to introduce a one-off windfall tax on utilities if it wins the next general elections, due by May 1997.
"We still don't know how that's going to be applied, but the electric and water utilities valuation levels seem to take that already into account," Davidson said.
Strategists say consumer demand driven sectors such as homebuilding, banks, and food and drink should see the sharpest earnings increases next year.
Manufacturing should also see a turnaround after a sluggish performance in 1996.
"This year has been driven by consumer demand. Next year, we would see some of that demand filtering back to the factories," said BZW's Bell.
